a: The Passover festival was about to begin
p: In John the last supper comes the day before Passover, and Jesus dies as the Passover lambs are killed.
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke call the last supper a Passover meal (Mark 14:12). John places it "before the Passover festival" and has Jesus die on "the day of preparation" (19:14, 31), the afternoon when the Passover lambs were slaughtered in the Temple. Scholars explain the difference in several ways: John changed the date to make a point about Jesus as the Lamb of God (1:29, 36; 19:36); John's date is the historical one and the Synoptics turned a farewell meal into a Passover (Raymond Brown and many others); Jesus followed a different calendar from the Temple, like the one used at Qumran (Annie Jaubert); or "Passover" here means the whole week-long festival, so both accounts can stand (D. A. Carson). No view has won everyone over.

a: cross over from this world to the Father
p: The verb means to pass from one place to another, a fitting word at Passover.
b: Metabainō means to move or cross over from one place to another. John uses it in 5:24 for passing "from death into life." Here it describes Jesus's death and return to the Father as a journey. At Passover the word has extra weight, because the festival remembered Israel's passing out of Egypt, and early Christian writers liked to connect the name pascha with "passing over." The whole second half of John, chapters 13 to 21, is the story of this crossing.
orig: μεταβῇ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου πρὸς τὸν πατέρα (metabē ek tou kosmou toutou pros ton patera)

a: he loved them all the way to the end
p: Eis telos can mean "until the end" of his life, or "to the uttermost." John probably means both.
b: The phrase eis telos has two senses in Greek: in time, "to the last," and in degree, "fully, to the limit." Jesus loved his disciples until his death, and he loved them as far as love can go. The same root returns at the cross, where Jesus's last word is tetelestai, "It is finished" or "It is complete" (19:30). The verb "loved" is an aorist, which can point to the single great act that follows: the foot washing and the death it acts out.
orig: εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτούς (eis telos ēgapēsen autous)

a: planted the plan in the heart
p: The Greek does not say whose heart: the devil's own, or Judas's. Many scholars think it means the devil's.
b: Word for word the Greek says: "the devil having already thrown into the heart that Judas should hand him over." Modern versions that say "of Judas" are interpreting; the KJV translates a different Greek word order (see the variant). But the grammar more naturally means that the devil had made up his own mind, "put it into his heart," that Judas would hand Jesus over (so Barrett and Brown). The Plain keeps the open wording. Either way the plot is now under way, and at 13:27 Satan himself goes into Judas.
orig: τοῦ διαβόλου ἤδη βεβληκότος εἰς τὴν καρδίαν (tou diabolou ēdē beblēkotos eis tēn kardian)

a: would hand Jesus over
p: Paradidōmi means to hand over. John uses it for Judas, for the Jewish leaders, for Pilate, and for Jesus himself.
b: Most English Bibles say Judas "betrayed" Jesus. The Greek paradidōmi is wider: to hand over, deliver up, give into someone's power. In John, Judas hands Jesus to the authorities (18:2, 5), the authorities hand him to Pilate (18:30, 35), Pilate hands him over to be crucified (19:16), and at the end Jesus "handed over his spirit" (19:30). Paul uses the same verb for God, who "handed him over for us all" (Romans 8:32). The Plain says "hand over" everywhere, so a reader can follow the chain.
orig: παραδοῖ (paradoi), from παραδίδωμι

a: set aside his outer clothes
p: The verbs are the ones Jesus used for laying down his life and taking it up again (10:17–18).
b: "Set aside" is tithēmi, the verb of the good shepherd who "lays down" his life (10:11, 15, 17–18). When Jesus finishes, he "took" his clothes again (13:12, elaben), the verb of 10:17–18: "I lay it down so that I may take it up again." Many commentators think John chose these words on purpose. The foot washing is an acted parable of the cross: the Lord strips, stoops to the work of a slave, cleanses his friends, and then takes up his clothes and his place again.
orig: τίθησιν τὰ ἱμάτια (tithēsin ta himatia)

a: started washing his disciples' feet
t: Washing feet in the ancient world
p: Guests' feet were washed on arrival, usually by slaves. A teacher washing his students' feet was unheard of.
b: People walked dusty roads in sandals, so a host offered water for the feet (Genesis 18:4; Luke 7:44). Usually a slave did the washing, or a wife for her husband, or children for a parent. Abigail offers to wash the feet of David's servants as a sign of lowliness (1 Samuel 25:41). A rabbinic commentary on Exodus, the Mekhilta (Nezikin 1, on Exodus 21:2), says that a Hebrew slave should not be made to wash his master's feet, because the task was too degrading even for him. Students served their teachers in many ways, but no one expected a teacher to wash his students. Jesus does it during the meal, not at the door, which shows it is a deliberate sign, not mere hospitality.

a: After this, you will know
p: John often says the disciples understood only after Easter (2:22; 12:16). The Spirit will remind them (14:26).
b: "After this" can mean in a few minutes, when Jesus explains (13:12–17), or after the cross and resurrection. John's pattern favors the second: "When he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered" (2:22; compare 12:16; 20:9). Jesus promises that the Spirit will bring his words back to their minds (14:26). The foot washing has two meanings, then: a lesson in humble service that they can grasp now, and a sign of the cleansing death that they will grasp only later.

a: you will have no share with me
p: Meros means a share or portion, the word for an inheritance. Refusing to be washed means refusing to belong.
b: Meros is a part or share. In the Greek Old Testament it is used for the share of the land each tribe received, and for the Levites, who had "no share" because the LORD was their share (Deuteronomy 12:12; 14:27). To have a share "with" Jesus is to belong with him and share what is his: his life, his place with the Father (14:3; 17:24). Peter's refusal is humble on the surface, but it would cut him off. Readers have taken the washing as a picture of Jesus's cleansing death, of baptism (Bultmann, Brown and Catholic interpreters in part), or of accepting the humiliation of a crucified Lord. These readings can stand together.
orig: οὐκ ἔχεις μέρος μετ' ἐμοῦ (ouk echeis meros met' emou)

a: Someone who has had a bath
p: Two different verbs: a full bath (louō) and washing a part (niptō). What is the bath?
b: Jesus uses louō, to bathe the whole body, and niptō, to wash hands or feet. A guest who had bathed at home only needed his feet washed on arrival. What is the "bath"? Augustine read it as baptism, after which Christians still need daily cleansing from sin (his Tractates on John 56), and Catholic and many Protestant readers follow a similar line. Others say the bath is Jesus's word (15:3) or his coming death, and the foot washing is simply that cleansing seen in a sign, so nothing more is needed. If the shorter text of Codex Sinaiticus is right (see the variant), the bath and the foot washing are the same thing.

a: you too owe it to one another to wash each other's feet
t: A debt, not only a suggestion
p: Opheilō means to owe. Jesus has put his disciples in his debt, and they repay it to each other.
b: The verb opheilō is the language of debt: "you are obliged." Jesus does not ask the disciples to wash his feet in return. They are to pay the debt sideways, to one another. 1 John uses the same verb: "we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers" (1 John 3:16). Whether the washing itself is to be repeated as a church rite, or only the humility it shows, is a question churches answer differently: see the card on this chapter. By the 300s some churches washed the feet of the newly baptized; Ambrose of Milan did so and noted that the church of Rome did not.
orig: ὀφείλετε (opheilete)

a: a slave does not rank above his master
p: A saying Jesus also uses in Matthew and Luke. Here it has a sharp point: if the master stoops, so must the slave.
b: The same saying appears in Matthew 10:24 and Luke 6:40, in other settings, and Jesus repeats it in 15:20. The Greek doulos means slave, not hired servant; many English Bibles soften it to "servant" because slavery is painful to read about, but the force here depends on it. The second half uses apostolos, "one who is sent," the word behind "apostle." It is the only time John's Gospel uses the word, and here it is a general word, not yet the title, so the Plain says "one who is sent." Jewish law knew the principle that "a man's agent is like the man himself" (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5): the messenger carries the authority of the sender, but never more.
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν δοῦλος μείζων τοῦ κυρίου αὐτοῦ, οὐδὲ ἀπόστολος (apostolos, "apostle," one who is sent) μείζων τοῦ πέμψαντος αὐτόν

a: 'The one who eats my bread has raised his heel against me.'
p: Jesus quotes David's complaint about a trusted friend who turned on him.
b: The quotation is Psalm 41:9, where David says of a close friend that he "has raised his heel high against me" (Psalm 41:9). John's Greek is his own, not the Septuagint's: he uses trōgō, "chew, eat," the vivid verb of 6:54–58, and leaves out the psalm's "the one I trusted," perhaps because Jesus knew from the start (6:64). Lifting the heel may picture a kick, or a horse rearing, or showing someone the sole of the foot, a deep insult in the Near East. Christian readers linked the psalm, and Jewish readers the similar Psalm 55, with Ahithophel, David's counselor who joined Absalom and later hanged himself (2 Samuel 15:12; 17:23), as Judas does in Matthew 27:5. Eating bread together created a bond of loyalty, which made the betrayal worse.
r: Psalm 41:9; Psalm 55:12–14; 6:54–58; 6:70–71; 2 Samuel 15:12; 2 Samuel 17:23; Matthew 26:23; Matthew 27:5; Acts 1:16

a: you will believe that I am
p: Jesus uses "I am" with no predicate, as in 8:24, 28, 58, echoing God's words in Isaiah 43:10.
b: Many versions add "he" ("that I am he"), and that is good English for "I am the one." But the Greek egō eimi stands alone, as in 8:24, 28, 58 and 18:5–8. The wording echoes the Greek of Isaiah 43:10, where God says, "so that you may know and believe and understand that I am," in a passage about God telling the future before it happens. That is exactly Jesus's point here: he tells them ahead of time, so that when it happens they will recognize who he is. Behind Isaiah stands God's self-naming to Moses (Exodus 3:14).
orig: ἵνα πιστεύσητε... ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι (hina pisteusēte... hoti egō eimi)

a: whoever takes in someone I send takes me in
p: The same chain of welcome appears in Matthew 10:40, at the sending of the Twelve.
b: Matthew 10:40 and Luke 10:16 have a similar saying when Jesus sends out his disciples. John places it here, right after the slave-and-messenger saying, to make clear that the disciples, though they must serve like slaves, carry the authority of the one who sends them, and through him of the Father. Even the one who hands Jesus over does not cancel this: the sending still stands.

a: Jesus was shaken in his spirit
p: The verb tarassō is used for Jesus at Lazarus's tomb and in 12:27. He then tells the disciples not to be shaken (14:1).
b: Tarassō means to stir up, agitate, disturb, as water is stirred in 5:7. John uses it of Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus (11:33), when his hour comes (12:27) and here. Then twice he tells the disciples, "Your heart must not be shaken" (14:1, 27). The Gospel that most stresses Jesus's divinity also shows him deeply moved. Jesus is shaken so that they need not be.
orig: ἐταράχθη τῷ πνεύματι (etarachthē tō pneumati)

a: reclining in Jesus' embrace
p: Guests lay on couches propped on the left elbow. The person to Jesus's right had his head near Jesus's chest.
b: At festive meals people did not sit on chairs. They lay on cushions or couches arranged in a U, leaning on the left elbow and eating with the right hand, feet stretched out behind (which made the foot washing possible). The Mishnah says that on Passover night even the poorest Israelite must not eat until he reclines (Mishnah Pesachim 10:1), which later rabbis explained as the posture of free people. The disciple next to Jesus could lean back against his chest (13:25). The word for "embrace" is kolpos, the same word used of the Son "in the Father's embrace" in 1:18: as Jesus is close to the Father and makes him known, this disciple is close to Jesus and makes him known (21:24).
orig: ἐν τῷ κόλπῳ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ (en tō kolpō tou Iēsou)

a: He was the one Jesus loved
p: His first appearance. Church tradition names John son of Zebedee; scholars suggest Lazarus, John the Elder and others.
b: This unnamed disciple appears from here on at key moments: at the cross (19:26–27), at the empty tomb (20:2–8), by the lake (21:7, 20–24), and perhaps as "the other disciple" in 18:15–16. The Gospel says he is its witness and source (19:35; 21:24). Irenaeus, in the late 100s, identified him as John the apostle, son of Zebedee, and most Christians have followed this. Other proposals: Lazarus, the only man the Gospel says Jesus loved by name (11:3, 5, 36); John the Elder, a Jerusalem disciple outside the Twelve (Martin Hengel; Richard Bauckham); or an ideal figure standing for the true disciple (Bultmann). He is never named, perhaps out of modesty, or so that every reader can stand in his place.

a: I will dip this bite of bread and give it to someone
p: Handing a guest a dipped piece of bread was a mark of favor. Jesus offers it to Judas.
b: At a meal the host might dip a piece of bread in a shared bowl of sauce and hand it to a guest as a sign of honor, as Boaz invited Ruth to dip her bread (Ruth 2:14). If Judas reclined at Jesus's left, the place of honor, the gesture would look like friendship to the others. That is why no one understands (13:28). In Matthew 26:23 and Mark 14:20, Jesus says the betrayer is the one who dips with him in the bowl; John alone has Jesus give the bread himself. Many readers see a final offer of love that Judas refuses.

a: Satan went into him
p: The devil prompts, Scripture foretells, and Jesus knows, yet Judas acts and is held responsible.
b: John holds several things together: the devil's plan (13:2), Scripture's prediction (13:18; 17:12), Jesus's foreknowledge (6:64, 70–71), and Judas's own choice and guilt; he is a thief (12:6). Luke also says that Satan entered Judas (Luke 22:3). Readers in the Reformed tradition see God's sovereign plan working through human wickedness without excusing it (Acts 2:23). Arminian and Orthodox readers stress that Judas freely opened himself to the devil, and that Jesus's offer of the bread was real. Some modern writers have tried to rehabilitate Judas as Jesus's obedient helper, but John gives no support to that idea.

a: give the poor something
t: Gifts to the poor at Passover
p: It was a custom to give to the poor at Passover, so the disciples thought nothing of it.
b: Judas kept the group's money box (12:6). Buying food at night was possible because Passover preparations went on late. Giving to the poor was a duty at the festival: the Mishnah says even a poor man must be given at least four cups of wine for the Passover meal (Mishnah Pesachim 10:1), and alms helped the poor buy what they needed. The disciples' guesses show how ordinary Judas's departure looked to everyone but Jesus and Judas.

a: It was night.
p: Three short words with a long shadow. In John, night is more than the time of day.
b: John has used light and darkness since the opening lines: "The light is shining in the dark" (1:5). Nicodemus came "by night" (3:2). Jesus warned that "the night is on its way, when nobody can work" (9:4) and that whoever walks at night stumbles (11:10; 12:35). Judas leaves the light of the world (8:12) and walks out into the dark. The phrase also sets the scene historically: the meal, the walk to the garden and the arrest all happen in one night.

a: Now the Son of Man has been glorified
p: In John, Jesus's death is his glory. With Judas gone, the events of the cross are already moving.
b: "Glorify" (doxazō) runs through chapters 12–17. For John, the cross is not a defeat that the resurrection has to reverse; it is itself the moment when God's glory, his true nature, shines out (12:23–28). The Son of Man is the figure of Daniel 7:13–14, who receives glory and rule from God. Isaiah's servant also "will be lifted up and glorified" in the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, just before the song of his suffering. The past tenses ("has been glorified") speak of what is about to happen as already done.
orig: νῦν ἐδοξάσθη ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (nyn edoxasthē ho huios tou anthrōpou)

a: Little children
p: Here begins a farewell address, a well-known form: a father or leader speaks to his own before death.
b: Jesus calls his disciples teknia, "little children," only here in the Gospel; 1 John uses it often (1 John 2:1, 12, 28). The tender word fits what follows, a farewell speech. The Bible and Jewish writings have many: Jacob blesses his sons (Genesis 49), Moses addresses Israel (Deuteronomy 31–33), Joshua and David give final charges (Joshua 23–24; 1 Kings 2:1–9), and the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs give each of Jacob's sons a deathbed speech. Such speeches announce the departure, comfort the hearers, give commands, warn of trouble ahead, name a successor and end in prayer. John 13:31–17:26 has every one of these features, and the successor is the Advocate.
r: Genesis 49; Deuteronomy 31–33; Joshua 23–24; 1 Kings 2:1–9; Acts 20:17–38; 1 John 2:1; 1 John 2:12; 1 John 2:28

a: What I said to the Jews
p: Jesus repeats to his disciples what he had said to the Jerusalem crowds in 7:34 and 8:21, but with a difference.
b: In 7:33–34 and 8:21 Jesus told his opponents in Jerusalem, called "the Jews," that they would look for him and not be able to come where he was going. Here "the Jews" again means those in Jerusalem who had argued with him, not the Jewish people as a whole: the disciples are Jews too. The same words now have a different future. For his opponents it was a warning; for the disciples it is temporary: "later on you will follow" (13:36), and he will come back to take them with him (14:3).

a: I am giving you a new command
p: Love of neighbor is as old as Leviticus 19:18. The new part is the measure, "as I loved you."
b: "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18) was already a summary of the law for Jewish teachers. Readers suggest several things that are new: the standard is no longer "as yourself" but "as I loved you," a love that lays down its life (15:13); it belongs to the new covenant that Jeremiah promised (Jeremiah 31:31–34); and it creates a new community whose love for each other is its badge (13:35). 1 John plays on this: it is an old command and yet a new one (1 John 2:7–8). In Latin this verse begins mandatum novum, and "Maundy" Thursday takes its name from mandatum, "command."

a: if you have love among yourselves
p: Some critics say John's love command is only for fellow believers. Others point to 3:16 and the mission to the world.
b: John speaks of love "for each other," not love of enemies (Matthew 5:44). Some scholars, such as Wayne Meeks and others who studied the "Johannine community," read this as the ethic of a small group under pressure that drew sharp lines around itself. Others answer that the love among disciples is meant to be seen by "all," and that it serves God's love for the whole world (3:16; 17:21, 23). Tertullian reports that pagans said of Christians, "See how they love one another" (Apology 39), which is just what this verse expects.

a: But later on you will follow
p: The promise is kept in 21:18–19, where Jesus hints at the death by which Peter will glorify God.
b: Peter cannot follow now, because Jesus's death is for others and must come first. Later he will follow, and the same verb returns in 21:19: "Follow me," after Jesus speaks of the death Peter will die. Early Christian writers report that Peter was martyred in Rome under Nero (1 Clement 5; Eusebius, Church History 2.25), and later tradition says he was crucified.

a: a rooster will not crow before you have denied me
p: Cockcrow was a time of night, the third watch. The prediction comes true in 18:27.
b: The Romans divided the night into four watches; the third was "cockcrow" (Mark 13:35), roughly midnight to three in the morning. The Mishnah says Jerusalemites were not to raise chickens in the city because of purity rules (Mishnah Bava Kamma 7:7), but whether that was kept, or whether foreign residents kept them, is uncertain, and roosters crow anyway. The prediction appears in all four Gospels (Matthew 26:34; Mark 14:30, with "twice"; Luke 22:34), and comes true in 18:17, 25–27. Peter is restored with three questions by the lake (21:15–17).

a: Put your trust in God, and put your trust in me as well
p: Both Greek verbs can be read as "you believe" or "believe!" so the line can be taken four ways.
b: The form pisteuete is the same for "you believe" and "believe!" The KJV takes the first as a statement and the second as a command: "ye believe in God, believe also in me." Most modern versions, and the Plain, take both as commands, which suits the setting: the disciples are frightened and need to be told to trust. The verse sets trust in Jesus alongside trust in God, a claim no ordinary teacher would make. "Heart" is singular in Greek, one shared heart of the group.
orig: πιστεύετε εἰς τὸν θεόν, καὶ εἰς ἐμὲ πιστεύετε (pisteuete eis ton theon, kai eis eme pisteuete)

a: many places to stay
p: The KJV's "mansions" comes from the Latin mansiones, "stopping places." It never meant big houses.
b: The Greek monai comes from menō, "remain, stay," the key verb of chapter 15. A monē is a place where one stays, a dwelling or lodging. The Latin Vulgate has mansiones, and the KJV's "mansions" meant dwellings in 1611, not luxury houses. "My Father's house" in 2:16 is the Temple, which had many rooms around it, and some scholars think Jesus pictures the heavenly temple (Mary Coloe). Origen read the "stopping places" as stages on the soul's journey to God. The same word returns in 14:23, where the Father and Son come to make their dwelling with the believer.
orig: μοναὶ πολλαί (monai pollai)

a: I am coming again
p: The Second Coming, the rapture, Easter, the Spirit, or the believer's death? Each has its readers.
b: Most Christians read this as the Second Coming at the end of the age (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Dispensationalists see in it a description of the rapture, when Christ takes the church to the Father's house before the tribulation (John Walvoord). Others note that in this same speech Jesus "comes" after Easter (14:18–19) and in the Spirit (14:23), and argue that John has turned the future coming into a present one (Bultmann; Dodd). Still others, especially in devotional writing, add that Jesus comes for each believer at death. Many commentators hold that John means more than one of these.

a: I am the way, the truth and the life
p: "The way" is the main idea; truth and life explain why Jesus is the way to the Father.
b: Thomas asked about the way, so "the way" is the main word, and "the truth and the life" say what kind of way: the true way that leads to life (or, as some put it, "the way because he is the truth and the life"). Israel's psalms ask God to "teach me your way" (Psalm 86:11), and the Dead Sea Scrolls call the community's life "the way." The first Christians were called "the Way" (Acts 9:2; 24:14). The second sentence makes Jesus the only route to the Father. Christians differ over whether people who have never heard of Jesus can still be saved through him; see the card on this chapter. Jewish readers, for whom the way to God is the Torah given at Sinai, have often felt this verse as a closed door.
r: 10:9; 1:18; Psalm 86:11; Acts 4:12; Acts 9:2; Acts 24:14; Hebrews 10:19–20; 1 Timothy 2:5

a: The one who has seen me has seen the Father
p: Moses was told no one can see God and live. John says the Father is seen in the Son.
b: God told Moses, "no human being can see me and stay alive" (Exodus 33:20), and John agrees that "Nobody has ever seen God" (1:18). Yet the only Son has made him known, so that to see Jesus is to see the Father. Paul calls Christ "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15), and Hebrews "the exact imprint of his nature" (Hebrews 1:3). The church fathers used this verse against those who made the Son a lesser being; Jewish readers note that the Bible also speaks of people who "saw the God of Israel" (Exodus 24:10) without that making anyone divine.

a: I am in the Father and the Father is in me
p: Each is "in" the other. Later theologians called this perichoresis, the Persons dwelling in one another.
b: John uses the little word "in" for a relationship of shared life: the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father (10:38; 14:10–11; 17:21), the believers in Jesus and Jesus in them (14:20; 15:4). Greek theologians, especially John of Damascus in the 700s, called the divine side of this perichōrēsis, a word picturing the Persons of the Trinity making room for one another. The Father "remains" in the Son and does his works through him, so Jesus's words and deeds are the Father's own.
orig: ἐγὼ ἐν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἐμοί (egō en tō patri kai ho patēr en emoi)

a: he will do greater ones than these
p: Greater in number and reach, through the church's mission after Jesus goes to the Father. Some expect greater miracles.
b: How can disciples do greater works than raising Lazarus? Most interpreters say "greater" in scope: after Jesus goes to the Father and sends the Spirit, the message spreads to the whole world, and more people are brought to life than in his ministry (Acts 2:41). Augustine argued that making a sinner righteous is a greater work than creating heaven and earth (Tractates on John 72). Pentecostal and charismatic Christians often read the verse as a promise of miracles in the church today. The reason given, "because I am on my way to the Father," ties the greater works to Jesus's glorification.

a: in my name
p: Not a formula to add to prayers. To ask in someone's name is to ask as his representative, for his purposes.
b: In the ancient world a person's name stood for the person and his authority. To act "in someone's name" was to act as his agent; Jewish law said "a man's agent is like the man himself" (Mishnah Berakhot 5:5). Asking in Jesus's name means asking as his people, in line with who he is and what he wants, so that "the Father will be glorified." The promise is repeated in 14:14; 15:7, 16; 16:23–26, always with conditions of remaining in him and his words.
orig: ἐν τῷ ὀνόματί μου (en tō onomati mou)

a: another Advocate
p: Paraklētos is someone called to stand beside you, a helper or defense lawyer. "Another" means Jesus was the first.
b: Paraklētos literally means "one called alongside." In Greek it was used for a supporter in court, a defense advocate or sponsor. Earlier English Bibles said "Comforter" (Wycliffe, Tyndale, KJV), from the Latin confortare, "to strengthen"; others say Helper or Counselor. The word passed into Hebrew: the Mishnah says that whoever does one commandment gains "one advocate" (peraqlit) for himself (Mishnah Avot 4:11). "Another Advocate" implies that Jesus has been their first one, and 1 John 2:1 calls Jesus our paraklētos with the Father. Some Muslim writers have read the promise as pointing to Muhammad (compare Quran 61:6); Christian interpreters reply that John identifies the Advocate as the Holy Spirit (14:26), who will be "in you."
orig: ἄλλον παράκλητον (allon paraklēton)

a: He is the Spirit of truth
p: The Dead Sea Scrolls also speak of a spirit of truth opposed to a spirit of deceit.
b: The Community Rule from Qumran (1QS 3–4) teaches that God set two spirits over humankind, a spirit of truth and a spirit of deceit, and that the sons of light walk in the first. John shares this vocabulary (1 John 4:6), but for John the Spirit of truth is not a force in every person; he is given to those who know Jesus and is closed to "the world." A small grammatical point: pneuma, "spirit," is neuter in Greek, so the pronouns in this verse are neuter. In 14:26, 15:26 and 16:13–14 John uses the masculine ekeinos, "that one," for the Spirit, and English Bibles say "he" throughout.

a: I will not abandon you like orphans
p: A teacher's students were his children. Plato says Socrates' followers felt like orphans when he was about to die.
b: Students called their teacher "father," and he called them his "children" (13:33). In Plato's Phaedo (116a), as Socrates prepares to drink the poison, his friends feel that they will spend the rest of their lives like orphans who have lost a father. Jesus promises the opposite: "I am coming to you." The coming may be his appearances after Easter (20:19), his presence through the Spirit, or both.

a: I live, so you too will live
p: The clause can explain why they will see him, or promise them life because he lives.
b: The Greek runs: "but you see me, because I live and you will live." The "because" (hoti) can look back ("you will see me because I am alive") or forward ("because I live, you also will live"). Most translations take it forward, as the Plain does. Either way the disciples' life depends on his: Easter is not only his return but the source of their own life (11:25–26).
orig: ὅτι ἐγὼ ζῶ καὶ ὑμεῖς ζήσετε (hoti egō zō kai hymeis zēsete)

a: Judas, not the Iscariot
p: Luke lists a "Judas son of James" among the Twelve. Some ancient Syriac versions call him Thomas.
b: Judas (Hebrew Judah) was a very common name. Luke's lists of the Twelve include "Judas son of James" (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13), who seems to match Thaddaeus in Matthew 10:3 and Mark 3:18. The Old Syriac versions of John name the speaker here as Thomas or "Judas Thomas," and in Syrian Christianity Thomas was often called Judas Thomas, "Judas the Twin." His question picks up the expectation that the Messiah would show himself publicly to the world (7:4).

a: make a place to stay with him
t: God makes his home with people
p: The word is monē, the same as the "places to stay" of 14:2. Here the Father and Son come to stay with the believer.
b: In 14:2 the disciples are promised places to stay in the Father's house. Here the movement runs the other way: the Father and the Son come and make their monē with whoever loves Jesus. The Old Testament promised that God would dwell among his people (Exodus 25:8; Ezekiel 37:27), and Revelation sees it at the end: "God's home is now with people" (Revelation 21:3). John says it begins now, for each one who keeps Jesus's word. Orthodox theology reads such verses as part of theosis, sharing in God's life.
orig: μονὴν παρ' αὐτῷ ποιησόμεθα (monēn par' autō poiēsometha)

a: he will bring back to your mind all that I told you
p: The Spirit will help the disciples remember and understand Jesus's words. Many see the Gospels themselves as the fruit.
b: The Gospel twice notes that the disciples remembered and understood only after the resurrection (2:22; 12:16). Here the Spirit is promised as the one who makes that happen. Many scholars see in this verse John's own account of how his Gospel came to be: the memories of an eyewitness, deepened and explained by the Spirit. Christians differ over how far the promise extends beyond the apostles: to their writings alone, or also to the church's continuing teaching. See the card on chapter 16.

a: I am leaving you peace
p: "Peace" was the everyday Jewish greeting and farewell. The world's peace was Rome's peace, kept by force.
b: Shalom was the ordinary word for hello and goodbye, and it also meant wholeness and well-being given by God (Numbers 6:26). The prophets promised a messianic peace (Isaiah 9:6–7; Ezekiel 37:26). "The way the world gives" may hint at the Pax Romana, the peace that Rome's emperors advertised on coins and monuments and enforced with legions. Jesus's peace is a gift, and it holds even in trouble (16:33). The risen Jesus greets the disciples with "Peace to you" (20:19, 21, 26).

a: the Father is greater than I am
t: Is the Son less than the Father?
p: A key verse in the debates of the 300s. Arius used it; the Nicene fathers gave several answers.
b: Arius and his followers used this verse to argue that the Son is a lesser, created being. Those who held to the Creed of Nicaea answered in two main ways. Some, like Gregory of Nazianzus, said the Father is "greater" as the source and cause of the Son, not in nature or rank (Oration 30.7). Others, like Augustine, said Jesus speaks here as a man: in his humanity he is less than the Father, while in his divinity he is equal (On the Trinity 1.7.14). The same Gospel says "I and the Father are one" (10:30) and calls the Son God (1:1; 20:28). Jehovah's Witnesses and Latter-day Saints read the verse as showing the Father's real superiority. See the card on this chapter.

a: In me he owns nothing
p: A Hebrew-style idiom: the ruler of this world has no rights over Jesus, no hold that would make his death deserved.
b: Literally "in me he has nothing." The phrase may reflect a Hebrew legal idiom, "he has nothing on me," meaning no claim, no case against me. Jesus is about to be arrested, but not because the devil has any power over him. He goes to his death freely, out of love and obedience to the Father (14:31; 10:18). John has called the devil "this world's ruler" in 12:31, where he is "thrown out," and will again in 16:11, where he "has already been judged."
orig: ἐν ἐμοὶ οὐκ ἔχει οὐδέν (en emoi ouk echei ouden)

a: Get up. Let us leave this place.
p: Jesus says "let us go," yet he speaks three more chapters before they leave (18:1). Why?
b: The words "Get up, let us go" are the same Greek as Jesus's words in Gethsemane in Mark 14:42, as he goes to meet the betrayer. In John, though, chapters 15–17 follow, and they leave only in 18:1. Proposals: the group got up and Jesus kept talking, perhaps on the way through the city (B. F. Westcott); the farewell speech grew in stages, and chapters 15–17 are a second version or later additions placed after an older ending (Brown, Bultmann, Lindars, Segovia); the pages of the Gospel were rearranged (J. H. Bernard); or the words are spiritual, "let us go out to meet the ruler of this world" (C. H. Dodd). Many literary readers now treat 13:31–17:26 as one carefully built unit whatever its history.

a: I am the real vine
p: In the Old Testament the vine is Israel. Jesus claims to be the vine himself, the true Israel.
b: Psalm 80 tells Israel's story as a vine: "A vine from Egypt you dug up and moved" (Psalm 80:8). Isaiah's song of the vineyard ends with God looking for good grapes and finding only rotten ones (Isaiah 5:1–7), and Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Hosea use the same picture for Israel's failure (Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15; 19:10–14; Hosea 10:1). A great golden vine hung over the entrance to the Temple's sanctuary (Josephus, Jewish War 5.210). When Jesus says "I am the real vine," he takes Israel's identity onto himself; his disciples belong to God's people by being joined to him. Some readers think the image was prompted by the cup of wine at supper, or by vineyards along the road to the Kidron valley.
r: Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Isaiah 27:2–6; Jeremiah 2:21; Ezekiel 15:1–8; Ezekiel 19:10–14; Hosea 10:1; Mark 12:1–12

a: real
p: Alēthinos means genuine, the real thing that others only pointed to: the real light, the real bread, the real vine.
b: John has a special word for "true": alēthinos, the genuine article as opposed to a copy or a shadow. Jesus is "the real light" (1:9), "the true bread" from heaven (6:32), and here the real vine. The point is not that Israel was a fake vine but that what Israel was meant to be finds its full reality in him. In 17:3 the Father is "the only real God."
orig: ἡ ἄμπελος ἡ ἀληθινή (hē ampelos hē alēthinē)

a: he takes away
p: Airō can mean "lift up" or "take away." A popular reading says God lifts fruitless branches off the ground.
b: The verb airō means to lift, carry off or remove. Some popular teachers (for example Bruce Wilkinson, Secrets of the Vine, 2001) argue that the farmer lifts sagging branches off the ground so they can bear fruit, a gentle care rather than judgment. Most commentators and vine experts reply that the context is cutting: in 15:6 the fruitless branch is thrown out and burned, and pruners in Judea cut away barren shoots in spring. The verse describes the fate of branches that are "in me" yet bear no fruit, which raises the question of perseverance (see 15:6).
orig: αἴρει αὐτό (airei auto)

a: he trims it clean
p: The word for pruning, kathairō, is the verb "to clean." Jesus then says, "You are clean already."
b: Greek writers on farming used kathairō, literally "clean," for clearing a vine of extra shoots. John chose it because of the next line: "You are clean (katharoi) already" (15:3), which recalls the foot washing: "You are clean, but not all of you are" (13:10). The disciples have already been pruned and cleansed by Jesus's word. Judas, the branch that bore no fruit, has gone out.
orig: καθαίρει αὐτό (kathairei auto)

a: Remain in me
p: Menō, "remain," appears eleven times in 15:1–17. The KJV says "abide."
b: Menō means to stay, remain, continue, live on. It is one of John's favorite words: the Spirit remained on Jesus (1:32–33), the first disciples asked where he was staying and remained with him (1:38–39), and those who eat his flesh remain in him (6:56). Here it becomes a command and a promise: remain in me, and I in you. The KJV's "abide" captures the sense of settled living. The word is related to the monai, "places to stay," of 14:2, 23. Fruit comes not from effort apart from Jesus but from staying joined to him, as a branch does nothing but stay in the vine.
orig: μείνατε ἐν ἐμοί (meinate en emoi)

a: throw them into the fire, and they burn
p: Does this describe believers who are lost, people who never truly belonged, or the loss of reward?
b: Vine wood is useless for building; Ezekiel says it is good only for fuel (Ezekiel 15:2–6). Christians read the warning in different ways. Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist and many Lutheran readers take it at face value: a real branch, really joined to Christ, can be cut off by refusing to remain, and the fire is final judgment. Reformed and many Baptist readers hold that those who are truly joined to Christ will persevere (10:28–29); the branch that is burned is someone outwardly attached, like Judas, whose lack of fruit shows he never truly lived from the vine. Some evangelicals see only a loss of reward or of fruitfulness. See the card on this chapter.

a: My Father is glorified in this
p: The Father's glory is seen in the fruit of the disciples' lives, as it was in the Son's work (17:4).
b: "Fruit" in John is not defined by a list. In context it includes love for one another (15:12), keeping Jesus's commands (15:10), prayer answered (15:7), and new believers brought in through their witness (4:36; 12:24; 15:16). The Father is glorified when the life of the vine shows in the branches, as he was glorified in the Son's finished work (17:4).

a: to lay down his life for the sake of his friends
p: Greek thinkers praised dying for a friend. Jesus says this is the greatest love, then does it.
b: The ideal of dying for one's friends was well known. In Plato's Symposium (179b) Phaedrus says that only lovers are willing to die for another, and Aristotle writes that a good man will even give his life for his friends (Nicomachean Ethics 9.8). Jesus uses the common ideal, then fills it with his own death the next day. Paul adds a twist: Christ died for us "while we were still sinners" and enemies (Romans 5:6–10). The phrase "lay down his life" ties this verse to the good shepherd (10:11) and to Peter's boast (13:37).

a: I do not call you slaves anymore
p: Abraham and Moses were God's friends. Jesus raises his disciples from slaves to friends who know his mind.
b: Doulos means slave, a person owned by another; many English Bibles say "servant," which hides how low the status was. A slave obeyed without being told why. A friend was let in on the plan. Abraham was called God's "friend" (Isaiah 41:8; 2 Chronicles 20:7; James 2:23), and God spoke with Moses "face to face, as anyone talks with a close companion" (Exodus 33:11). At royal courts, "Friend of the King" was a rank for trusted advisers. The disciples still obey (15:14), and in 15:20 Jesus repeats the slave saying, but they now obey as friends who know what their master is doing.
orig: οὐκέτι λέγω ὑμᾶς δούλους... ὑμᾶς δὲ εἴρηκα φίλους (ouketi legō hymas doulous... hymas de eirēka philous)

a: It was not you who chose me
p: Jesus chose the Twelve for a mission. Christians differ on whether the verse also teaches election to salvation.
b: In Jesus's world, students chose their rabbi. Here the reverse is stressed: Jesus chose them (6:70; 13:18), and "put them in place" (the same verb tithēmi as laying down a life) to go and bear lasting fruit. Many readers, especially Arminian and Wesleyan ones, take this as choice for a task, apostleship and mission, since Judas too was chosen (6:70). Reformed readers see in it a pattern of God's gracious initiative in salvation as well (6:44; 17:6). Both agree that the disciples' relationship with Jesus starts with his choice, not their merit.

a: If the world hates you
p: Kosmos in John can mean the created world, humanity that God loves, or human society organized against God.
b: John uses kosmos 78 times. God made it (1:10) and loves it (3:16); Jesus came to save it (3:17; 12:47). But it also means humanity as it shuts God out: it "did not know him" (1:10), it hates Jesus because he exposes its works (7:7), and its ruler is the devil (14:30). In this section, 15:18–16:4, the world is the hostile setting in which the disciples must live and witness. They are not taken out of it (17:15), but they no longer "come from" it.
orig: ὁ κόσμος (ho kosmos)

a: If they hunted me down, they will hunt you down too
p: The Gospel's first readers knew this from experience: exclusion from synagogues, hostility from neighbors, Roman trials.
b: Diōkō means to pursue, chase, persecute. Acts records the arrest of the apostles, the stoning of Stephen and the killing of James (Acts 4–5; Acts 7; Acts 12:2). By the time John wrote, Christians in the Roman province of Asia faced local hostility and occasional trials; around AD 112 Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, wrote to the emperor Trajan about executing Christians who would not curse Christ (Pliny, Letters 10.96). Jesus prepares the disciples so that the hatred will not surprise them or make them stumble (16:1, 4).

a: they would have no sin
t: The sin of rejecting the light
p: Not that they had no sins at all. John means the sin of refusing Jesus once he had come and spoken.
b: In John, "sin" in the singular often means the basic refusal to believe in Jesus (16:9). Those who never heard would not be guilty of that refusal; those who heard and saw have no "cover" (prophasis, pretext, excuse). Compare 9:41: "If you were blind, you would have no sin." The same principle, that responsibility grows with knowledge, appears in Luke 12:47–48 and Romans 2:12.
orig: ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ εἴχοσαν (hamartian ouk eichosan)

a: 'They hated me for no reason.'
p: The words come from the Psalms. "Their law" sounds distancing, as if Jesus were not a Jew.
b: The quotation matches Psalm 35:19 and Psalm 69:4, "Those who hate me without a cause" (Psalm 69:4), both psalms of a righteous sufferer; Psalm 69 is quoted elsewhere of Jesus (2:17; 19:28–29). "Law" here means Scripture in general, as in 10:34 and 12:34. Jesus, a Jew, calls it "their law," which has struck many readers as a sign that John wrote after Christians and synagogues had separated (compare 8:17; 10:34). Others note that it means "the very law they claim to follow," a sharp argument from their own Scripture. Either way, these lines were later used to set Christians against Jews, a use the Gospel's own Jewish characters would not recognize.

a: who proceeds from the Father
p: The verb here, ekporeuomai, became the word of the Nicene Creed: the Spirit "proceeds from the Father."
b: Jesus says he will send the Advocate "from the Father," and that the Spirit "proceeds" (ekporeuetai) from the Father. The Plain keeps "proceeds" for this verb so that it is not confused with exerchomai, "come out," used of the Son in 16:27–28. The Creed of Constantinople (381) took these words: the Spirit "proceeds from the Father." Latin churches later added "and the Son" (filioque), first in Spain (Toledo, 589) and at Rome in the 1000s. The Orthodox objected that the Creed was changed without a council and that the verse distinguishes the Spirit's eternal origin from the Father alone from his being sent in time by the Son. Western theologians reply that the Son sends the Spirit (15:26; 16:7) and that the Spirit takes from what is the Son's (16:14–15). Many scholars think John himself is speaking of the Spirit's mission, not of eternal relations. See the card on this chapter.
orig: ὃ παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἐκπορεύεται (ho para tou patros ekporeuetai)

a: You too are witnesses
p: The verb can be a statement or a command. Witness is a courtroom word, and in time it came to mean martyr.
b: Martyreite can mean "you are witnesses" or "be witnesses!" Both fit: they have been with Jesus "since the start" and so are qualified witnesses, and they are sent to testify. The Spirit and the disciples testify together, as in Acts 5:32: "We ourselves are witnesses of these events. The Holy Spirit is a witness too." The whole Gospel is built like a trial, with witnesses for Jesus (5:31–39). The Greek martys, "witness," later came to mean someone who witnessed by dying: a martyr.
orig: καὶ ὑμεῖς δὲ μαρτυρεῖτε (kai hymeis de martyreite)

a: tripped up
p: Skandalizō means to trip someone or make them fall. Jesus warns them so the coming trouble will not destroy their faith.
b: A skandalon was the trigger of a trap or a stone that trips the foot. To be "scandalized" is to have one's faith tripped and brought down. The same verb appears in 6:61, when many disciples were offended by Jesus's words and left. Here the danger is persecution: if the disciples know in advance that hatred is coming, it will not knock them over.
orig: ἵνα μὴ σκανδαλισθῆτε (hina mē skandalisthēte)

a: They will throw you out of the synagogue
p: One of three places John uses aposynagōgos. Scholars debate what real event, if any, lies behind it.
b: The word aposynagōgos, "expelled from the synagogue," appears only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). J. Louis Martyn argued that it reflects the Gospel's own time, when, he thought, a synagogue prayer against heretics, the Birkat ha-Minim, was used to expel Jews who confessed Jesus. Many scholars now doubt that link: the prayer's date and target are uncertain, and it was probably not aimed at Christians as such (Reuven Kimelman; Daniel Boyarin). Others think local expulsions happened without any empire-wide decree, as Paul's own punishments in synagogues suggest (2 Corinthians 11:24). Adele Reinhartz warns that the Gospel itself, read uncritically, has taught Christians to see Jews as persecutors, while history later ran the other way.

a: anyone who kills you will think he is offering worship to God
p: Saul of Tarsus is the clearest example: he hunted Christians out of zeal for God.
b: Latreia is the word for worship and Temple service. Paul later described himself as a zealous persecutor of the church (Galatians 1:13–14; Philippians 3:6; Acts 26:9–11), and Acts tells of Stephen's stoning (Acts 7:57–60). Zeal that kills in God's name had a model in Phinehas (Numbers 25:7–13). The warning also cuts against later Christians, who killed Jews and other Christians in the belief that they were serving God. Jesus's point is that religious sincerity is no proof of knowing the Father (16:3).
orig: λατρείαν προσφέρειν τῷ θεῷ (latreian prospherein tō theō)
r: 16:3; Galatians 1:13–14; Philippians 3:6; Acts 7:57–60; Acts 26:9–11; Numbers 25:7–13; Romans 10:2

a: not one of you asks me
t: But Peter and Thomas did ask
p: Peter asked "Where are you going?" in 13:36, and Thomas in 14:5. Why does Jesus say no one asks?
b: This is one of the seams that lead many scholars to think the farewell speech grew in layers (see the note on 14:31): 16:4b–33 may be a parallel version of the themes of chapter 14, composed separately. Others read it in context: earlier the disciples asked only about their own loss; now, filled with grief, they are not asking the question that would comfort them, where he is going, which is to the Father, for their good (16:7).

a: you are better off if I go away
p: Sympherei means "it is to your advantage." Caiaphas used the same word: better that one man die (11:50).
b: The verb sympherei appears in 11:50 and 18:14, when Caiaphas says it is "better for you" that one man die for the people. John lets the echo stand: Jesus's going, through death, is indeed to their advantage, but in a way Caiaphas did not mean. The Spirit could not be given until Jesus was glorified (7:39); after the resurrection Jesus breathes the Spirit on them (20:22).
orig: συμφέρει ὑμῖν (sympherei hymin)

a: expose the world's error
p: Elenchō is a courtroom word: to cross-examine, to prove guilty, to show someone up.
b: Elenchō can mean to bring to light (3:20), to convict of guilt (8:46), or to prove someone wrong. The world put Jesus on trial and condemned him; now the Spirit will put the world on trial and show that it was wrong on three counts: about sin, about righteousness and about judgment. Translations divide between "convict" (KJV "reprove") and "prove wrong." The three short explanations that follow (16:9–11) are famously hard; each begins with "because" or "that" (hoti), which the Plain renders with a colon.
orig: ἐλέγξει τὸν κόσμον (elenxei ton kosmon)

a: About righteousness
p: Jesus's going to the Father proves he was in the right. Or it exposes the world's false righteousness.
b: Two main readings: (1) The Spirit shows that Jesus, condemned as a sinner, was righteous, and the proof is that the Father has taken him back (Brown and many). (2) The Spirit exposes the world's own righteousness as empty, since the world thought it was serving God by condemning him (16:2; Carson). Luther and the Reformers read it as the righteousness that Christ gives to believers by faith. The phrase "you no longer see me" suggests that, with Jesus gone, the Spirit takes up his case.

a: this world's ruler has already been judged
p: At the cross the devil, not Jesus, is condemned. The verdict is passed already.
b: The perfect tense kekritai means "has been judged and stands condemned." In 12:31 Jesus said "now this world's ruler will be thrown out," and in 14:30 that he "owns nothing" in Jesus. The cross that looks like the world's verdict on Jesus is God's verdict on the devil. Paul says the same in another picture: God "disarmed the rulers and authorities" through the cross (Colossians 2:15).
orig: κέκριται (kekritai)

a: it would be too heavy for you to carry
p: Bastazō means to carry a load. Jesus does not tell them everything because they could not bear it yet.
b: The verb bastazō is used of carrying the cross in 19:17. The disciples cannot yet carry the weight of what he would say, perhaps about his death, the mission to the nations or the suffering ahead. The Spirit will lead them later (16:13). The verse has been used in many directions: by Montanists and others to claim new revelations, and by churches to explain how doctrine developed. Most interpreters tie it closely to what Jesus has already said: the Spirit will "take from what is mine" (16:14).
orig: οὐ δύνασθε βαστάζειν ἄρτι (ou dynasthe bastazein arti)

a: he will lead you in all the truth
p: A promise to the apostles, to the whole church, or to every believer? Churches answer differently.
b: Hodēgeō means to lead along a road, as in Psalm 25:5, where the Greek (Psalm 24:5 in the Septuagint) has "lead me to your truth." It picks up "the way" of 14:6. Christians agree that the Spirit led the apostles. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that the promise also guards the church's teaching through the centuries, in councils and (for Catholics) the teaching office of the bishops with the pope. Protestants generally read it as fulfilled in the apostles' witness now written in the New Testament, by which all later teaching is tested, while also praying for the Spirit's light on every reader. See the card on this chapter.
orig: ὁδηγήσει ὑμᾶς ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πάσῃ (hodēgēsei hymas en tē alētheia pasē)

a: the things that are coming
p: Future events in general, the events of the cross and resurrection, or the whole new age the Spirit opens.
b: Some read "the things that are coming" as prophecy of the future, such as the visions of Revelation. Others think of the events just ahead, Jesus's death and resurrection, which the Spirit will explain. Still others take it broadly: the Spirit will interpret the new situation of the church after Jesus's departure. In context the Spirit does not bring a separate message but will "take from what is mine" (16:14).

a: Everything the Father has belongs to me
p: The fathers used this verse for the full equality of the Son, and it became part of the Filioque debate.
b: Athanasius and the Cappadocian fathers cited this verse to show that the Son shares everything that is the Father's except being the Father. Latin theologians from Augustine onward used it with 16:14 to argue that the Spirit receives from the Son as well as from the Father, the basis of the filioque (see the note on 15:26). Orthodox theologians answer that the verse is about the Spirit's work of revealing Christ, not his eternal origin. The verse also has a simple pastoral point: when the Spirit makes Jesus known, he makes the Father known.

a: A short time, and you no longer see me
p: Most read the two "short times" as Jesus's death and resurrection. Some include the time until his return.
b: Mikron, "a little," is repeated seven times in 16:16–19, as the disciples puzzle over it. The first "short time" ends with his death the next day. The second ends with the resurrection appearances, when they see him and rejoice (20:20). Some interpreters, noting "that day" (16:23, 26) and the image of birth pains (16:21), also hear the Second Coming. John may want both: Easter joy is a foretaste of the end.

a: When a woman is in labor
p: Israel's prophets used labor pains for the anguish before God's new age. The word for "pain" is the same as "grief."
b: The prophets compared Israel's distress to a woman in labor (Isaiah 26:17–18; Jeremiah 30:6–7) and pictured Zion giving birth to a new people (Isaiah 66:7–14). Jewish writings spoke of the "birth pains of the Messiah," the suffering before the new age, and Jesus uses the image for the end in Mark 13:8. Here the pains are the disciples' grief at his death, and the birth is his resurrection and the new life it brings. "Her hour has come" echoes Jesus's own "hour." In Greek "pain" is lypē, the word translated "grief" in 16:6, 20 and 22.
r: Isaiah 26:17–19; Isaiah 66:7–14; Jeremiah 30:6–7; Micah 4:9–10; Mark 13:8; Romans 8:22; Revelation 12:2; 13:1; 17:1

a: you will not ask me any questions
p: Erōtaō, ask a question, and aiteō, ask for something, sit side by side in this verse.
b: The first "ask" (erōtaō) looks back to 16:19, where the disciples wanted to ask Jesus what he meant. After Easter they will no longer need to ply him with questions. The second "ask" (aiteō) means to request: prayer to the Father in Jesus's name. Some interpreters think John uses the two verbs loosely, since erōtaō can also mean "request" (16:26; 17:9), but the change of verbs within one sentence suggests the difference matters here.
orig: ἐμὲ οὐκ ἐρωτήσετε οὐδέν... ἄν τι αἰτήσητε (eme ouk erōtēsete ouden... an ti aitēsēte)

a: in word pictures
p: Paroimia is a proverb, a dark saying or figure of speech, like Hebrew mashal. John uses it for the shepherd talk (10:6).
b: A paroimia is a saying whose meaning is not plain: a proverb, a parable, a riddle. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Hebrew mashal (Proverbs 1:1 in some Greek versions). John calls the good shepherd speech a paroimia (10:6), and the Plain uses "word picture" in both places. Jesus admits that much of what he has said is veiled; after the resurrection he will speak "openly" (parrēsia, boldly, plainly), likely through the Spirit. In 16:29 the disciples think that time has already come, but their confident faith is about to scatter (16:32).
orig: ἐν παροιμίαις (en paroimiais)

a: I do not tell you that I will ask the Father for you
p: Elsewhere Jesus intercedes for his people (17:9; Romans 8:34). Here the point is the Father's own love.
b: This verse seems to clash with chapter 17, where Jesus does pray for the disciples, and with texts that show the risen Christ interceding (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25; 1 John 2:1). Most interpreters say Jesus is correcting a wrong picture: the disciples need not imagine an unwilling Father who must be persuaded by the Son, because the Father himself loves them (16:27). Their prayer "in my name" already unites them with the Son, and in him they come straight to the Father.

a: the Father himself loves you
p: Here the verb for love is phileō, not agapaō. John uses both for God's love, which matters for 21:15–17.
b: Both the Father's love and the disciples' love here use phileō. Elsewhere John uses agapaō for the same relationships: the Father loves the Son with agapaō in 3:35 and with phileō in 5:20. This suggests that John uses the two verbs as near-synonyms. That bears on the famous exchange in 21:15–17, where Jesus asks Peter twice with agapaō and once with phileō. Some preachers make a sharp contrast there between divine and human love; many scholars, citing passages like this one, doubt that John intends it.
orig: αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ πατὴρ φιλεῖ ὑμᾶς (autos gar ho patēr philei hymas)

a: you will scatter
p: Mark and Matthew quote Zechariah 13:7 here: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will scatter.
b: In Mark 14:27 and Matthew 26:31 Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7, "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." John does not quote it but uses the same verb (skorpizō) as in 10:12, where the wolf scatters the sheep. Yet in John's arrest scene Jesus asks the soldiers to let the disciples go (18:8–9). The flight is real, but Jesus is not alone: the Father is with him. Compare the cry from Psalm 22:1 in Mark 15:34, which John does not include.

a: I have won the victory over the world
p: Nikaō, to conquer or win. The perfect tense speaks of a victory already won, the night before the cross.
b: Jesus speaks of his victory as already complete: nenikēka, "I have conquered and the victory stands." The same verb is the key word of 1 John 5:4–5 ("this is the victory that has conquered the world, our faith") and of Revelation's promises "to the one who wins the victory" (Revelation 2:7). Jesus does not promise his followers escape from hardship (thlipsis, pressure, affliction) but peace in him and a share in his victory.
orig: ἐγὼ νενίκηκα τὸν κόσμον (egō nenikēka ton kosmon)
r: 1 John 5:4–5; 1 John 4:4; Revelation 2:7; Revelation 3:21; Revelation 5:5; Romans 8:37; 14:27

a: he raised his eyes toward heaven
p: Jesus prays aloud with eyes lifted, a common Jewish posture. Since the 1500s it is called the High Priestly Prayer.
b: Jews usually prayed standing with eyes and hands lifted (11:41; Psalm 123:1; compare Luke 18:13, where the tax collector will not lift his eyes). The prayer is spoken in the disciples' hearing, so it is meant for them too (11:42). The Lutheran theologian David Chytraeus (1530 or 1531–1600) is usually credited with calling it the "High Priestly Prayer," because Jesus consecrates himself and intercedes for his people like a priest (17:19). Others call it the prayer of consecration or the Lord's own prayer. It falls into three parts: for himself (17:1–5), for the disciples (17:6–19), and for all who will believe (17:20–26).

a: Father, the hour has arrived
p: Throughout John the hour "had not yet come" (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Since 12:23 it has arrived.
b: At Cana Jesus said, "My hour is not here yet" (2:4), and twice his enemies could not arrest him "because his hour had not yet come" (7:30; 8:20). When Greeks came to see him, he said the hour had come for the Son of Man to be glorified (12:23). In 13:1 the hour is the time to cross over to the Father. Now, at the edge of the cross, he prays: the hour is here. The hour is his death, resurrection and return to the Father seen as one event, his glorification.
orig: ἐλήλυθεν ἡ ὥρα (elēlythen hē hōra)

a: authority over all people
p: Literally "all flesh," a Hebrew way of saying every human being. "All that you have given him" is neuter in Greek.
b: "All flesh" (Hebrew kol basar) means all humankind (Genesis 6:12; Isaiah 40:5). The authority recalls the Son of Man in Daniel 7:14, given "authority" over all peoples. In the second half the Greek uses a neuter singular, "all that you have given him," for the disciples as a whole, the same pattern as 6:37, 39 and 17:24, picturing them as one gift from the Father to the Son.
orig: ἐξουσίαν πάσης σαρκός... πᾶν ὃ δέδωκας αὐτῷ (exousian pasēs sarkos... pan ho dedōkas autō)

a: Eternal life is this
p: Eternal life is defined as knowing God and Jesus Christ. Christians and others read "the only real God" differently.
b: This is the nearest John comes to a definition: eternal life, "the life of the age to come," is to know God, in the full Hebrew sense of knowing a person (Jeremiah 31:34; Hosea 6:6). It echoes Israel's Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4). The use of the full name "Jesus Christ" in Jesus's own mouth is unusual (elsewhere only 1:17), and many scholars think the evangelist's wording shows through. Jehovah's Witnesses cite the verse to show that only the Father is God. Augustine and Nicene Christians read it as "that they may know you and the one you sent, Jesus Christ, as the only true God," or note that knowing Jesus is placed beside knowing God as the content of eternal life, which no creature could claim.

a: the glory I had beside you before there was a world
p: Jesus speaks of a glory he shared with the Father before the world began, as in 1:1 and 8:58.
b: The Gospel opened with the Word who "was with God" in the beginning (1:1–2). Here Jesus prays to return to the glory he had "beside" the Father before creation. Jewish wisdom writings said Wisdom was beside God before the world (Proverbs 8:22–31; Wisdom of Solomon 9:9–10), and early Christians applied such language to Jesus (Philippians 2:6; Colossians 1:15–17). Isaiah has God say, "I will not hand my glory to another" (Isaiah 42:8), which makes the claim striking. Readers who deny Jesus's pre-existence read it as glory planned for him in God's mind.

a: I have brought your name into the open
p: In the Bible a name reveals a person. Jesus has shown who God is. Some think the name given to Jesus is "I am."
b: Phaneroō means to make visible. God's "name" is his revealed character and presence (Exodus 34:5–7; Deuteronomy 12:5). Jesus has shown the disciples who God really is: Father. In 17:11–12 he speaks of "your name, the name you have given me," and scholars ask which name that is. Suggestions include "I am" (8:58; 13:19), "Lord" (Philippians 2:9–11) or simply "Father." Isaiah promised that God's people would one day know his name (Isaiah 52:6).
orig: ἐφανέρωσά σου τὸ ὄνομα (ephanerōsa sou to onoma)

a: It is not the world I am asking for
p: Jesus prays here for the disciples, but the goal is that the world will believe (17:21, 23).
b: At first this sounds cold. But it describes the focus of this part of the prayer: the disciples who will be left in the world. Later Jesus prays for all who will believe through them, so that "the world will believe" and "know" (17:21, 23). The God who loved the world (3:16) reaches it through those he keeps and sends (17:18). Reformed readers have also used the verse for the doctrine that Christ's intercession is for the elect.

a: Holy Father
p: This address is unique in the Gospels. The Didache's early communion prayer, from about AD 100, uses it too.
b: Jesus calls God simply "Father" (17:1, 5, 21, 24), "Righteous Father" (17:25) and here "Holy Father," holiness being the theme of this part of the prayer (17:17, 19). The Didache, a church manual from about AD 100, gives a thanksgiving after the meal that begins: "We thank you, holy Father, for your holy name which you made to dwell in our hearts" (Didache 10:2), very close to John 17 in its themes of name, keeping and unity. Today "Holy Father" is also a title of the pope, a later use that has nothing to do with this verse.
orig: πάτερ ἅγιε (pater hagie)

a: the son of ruin
p: A pun: none was ruined except the "son of ruin." A Hebrew idiom for someone who belongs to destruction.
b: "Son of" in Hebrew idiom means "one who belongs to" or "one marked by." The Greek plays on apōleto, "was ruined, lost," and apōleia, "ruin, destruction." Paul uses the same phrase for the "man of lawlessness" (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so some readers link Judas with the antichrist. "So that the Scripture would come true" probably points back to Psalm 41:9 (13:18); Acts 1:16–20 adds Psalms 69 and 109. The verse does not settle whether Judas was predestined to fall; see the note on 13:27.
orig: ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας (ho huios tēs apōleias)

a: keep them safe from the evil one
p: Tou ponērou can be "the evil one" or "evil." John's letters point to the devil.
b: The genitive tou ponērou could be masculine, "the evil one," or neuter, "evil." The same ambiguity sits in the Lord's Prayer, "deliver us from evil" or "from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13). In John's letters the evil one is clearly the devil: "the whole world lies in the power of the evil one" (1 John 5:19; compare 1 John 2:13–14; 5:18), so most scholars read it that way here. Jesus does not pray for escape from the world but for protection in it.
orig: τηρήσῃς αὐτοὺς ἐκ τοῦ πονηροῦ (tērēsēs autous ek tou ponērou)

a: Make them holy in the truth
p: Hagiazō means to set apart for God, as priests and sacrifices were. Jesus sets himself apart for his death (17:19).
b: Hagiazō means to make holy or set apart for God's use. In the Greek Old Testament it is used for consecrating priests (Exodus 28:41; 29:1) and for sacrifices and firstborn animals given to God (Deuteronomy 15:19). In 10:36 the Father "made holy and sent" the Son. In 17:19 Jesus says, "I make myself holy," that is, he dedicates himself as an offering, the language of priest and sacrifice at once. The disciples are set apart "in the truth," the word of God, so that they can be sent as he was (17:18).
orig: ἁγίασον αὐτοὺς ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ (hagiason autous en tē alētheia)
r: 10:36; 17:19; Exodus 28:41; Exodus 29:1; Deuteronomy 15:19; Hebrews 10:10; Hebrews 10:14; Ephesians 5:26

a: in the same way I sent them into the world
p: The mission pattern of John: the Father sends the Son, the Son sends the disciples (20:21).
b: John calls the Father "the one who sent me" more than twenty times. Here the sending passes on: as the Father sent the Son, the Son sends the disciples. The past tense "I sent" looks ahead to 20:21, where the risen Jesus says, "As the Father has sent me, I am sending you," and breathes the Spirit on them. They are sent into the same world that hated him (15:18–21).

a: those who believe in me through what they say
p: Jesus prays for all future believers, including the readers of this Gospel.
b: "What they say" is literally "their word," the apostles' witness. Later readers of John, who did not see Jesus (20:29), are included in this prayer, which is part of the Gospel's purpose: "so that you may believe" (20:31). Christians of every age have read this verse as Jesus praying for them personally.

a: so that all of them will be one
t: That they may all be one
p: The motto of the modern movement for Christian unity. Churches differ on what kind of unity Jesus meant.
b: In Latin, ut omnes unum sint, "that all may be one," became the motto of the ecumenical movement, and Pope John Paul II's 1995 encyclical on unity is titled Ut Unum Sint. Catholics and Orthodox understand the unity as visible: one church with shared sacraments and ministry. Many Protestants see it first as a spiritual unity of all true believers, shown in love and cooperation across denominations. All agree that the model is the unity of the Father and the Son, and the purpose is mission: "Then the world will believe."

a: let them also be in us
p: Believers are drawn into the life of the Father and the Son. Orthodox theology calls this theosis.
b: Jesus prays not only that believers be united with each other, but that they be "in us," within the shared life of the Father and the Son. With 17:22–23 ("I in them and you in me") and 2 Peter 1:4 ("sharers in the divine nature"), Eastern Orthodox theology reads this as theosis: by grace people come to share God's life without becoming God by nature. Western traditions speak of union with Christ and adoption as children. Both reject the idea that humans dissolve into God.

a: made complete as one
p: Teleioō means to bring to completion or maturity. Their unity is a goal still being reached.
b: The perfect passive participle teteleiōmenoi means "brought to completion," and eis hen means "into one." It is the verb of 4:34, 5:36 and 17:4, where Jesus completes the Father's work, and of 19:28, where Scripture is fulfilled. The disciples' unity is not finished all at once but brought toward its goal. The world's coming to know the Father's love depends on it.
orig: ἵνα ὦσιν τετελειωμένοι εἰς ἕν (hina ōsin teteleiōmenoi eis hen)

a: since you loved me before the world was founded
t: Love before the foundation of the world
p: The love between Father and Son is older than creation. The New Testament also speaks of believers chosen before it.
b: The phrase "before the world was founded" (pro katabolēs kosmou) appears also in Ephesians 1:4 (God chose us in Christ) and 1 Peter 1:20 (Christ was foreknown). Here it describes the eternal love of the Father for the Son, the source from which the love for the disciples flows (17:23, 26). Jesus's wish is that his people will see his glory, the hope of 14:3 and of Revelation 22:4.

a: I will go on letting them know it
p: Jesus will keep revealing the Father, through the cross and then through the Spirit.
b: The prayer ends where the farewell speech began, with love. Jesus has made the Father's name known and will go on doing so: first through his death and resurrection, the fullest showing of the Father's love, and then through the Spirit, who will teach and remind (14:26; 16:13–15). The last words, "I will be in them," sum up the whole discourse: the departing Jesus will be present in his people.
